subject: psychology
topic: Multitasking is switching, and every switch costs you
angle: While heavy media multitaskers are linked to worse task-switching ability due to interference, they actually show an increased ability to shift between discrete tasks in specific experimental paradigms.
title: The Cost of Constant Switching

hooks.text: Does your phone make you faster at switching tasks?
You think multitasking hurts your focus. The evidence is mixed.
You are training your brain to filter out the world.
A blue light glow in a dark room.

reveal.headline: Heavy media multitasking may improve your ability to switch tasks.
reveal.body: While it may hurt your focus, research shows heavy media multitaskers can sometimes switch between discrete tasks more effectively than light multitaskers. The evidence on this is mixed and contested.

explain.headline: Your brain is adapting to constant distraction.
explain.body: Media multitasking is linked to a reduced ability to filter out irrelevant information. This creates interference. However, it also shows positive effects on your attitudes toward your digital habits.

matters.headline: Your cognitive architecture is shifting.
matters.body: That may be why you feel faster at moving between apps but find it harder to ignore the noise of the world. Your brain is evolving new strategies for a fragmented life.

example.headline: A phone on a desk during a meeting.
example.body: You glance at a notification while listening to a coworker. You return to the speaker. You do this every hour.

question.headline: Is your brain getting faster or just more distracted?

stat.label: the effect of media multitasking on task-switching ability

claims.text: Heavy media multitaskers were better able to switch between tasks in the task-switching paradigm than light media multitaskers.
claims.quote: Across 2 experiments, heavy media multitaskers were better able to switch between tasks in the task-switching paradigm.

claims.text: Heavy media multitaskers are linked to a reduced ability to filter out interference from irrelevant tasks, which makes them perform worse on a test of task-switching ability.
claims.quote: heavy media multitaskers performed worse on a test of task-switching ability, likely due to reduced ability to filter out interference from the irrelevant task set.

claims.text: Heavy and light media multitaskers showed comparable performance in the dual-task.
claims.quote: Heavy and light media multitaskers showed comparable performance in the dual-task.

claims.text: Media multitasking has negative effects on cognitive outcomes, but it has positive effects on attitudinal outcomes.
claims.quote: this meta-analysis showed that multitasking has negative effects on cognitive outcomes, whereas it has positive effects on attitudinal (or persuasion-related) outcomes.

claims.text: The association between media multitasking and cognitive control is small across measurement approaches and cognitive control functions.
claims.quote: Overall, the pooled effect size of the association, across measurement approaches and cognitive control functions, is small.

claims.text: As task-switching costs rise, groups increasingly evolve division of labor strategies.
claims.quote: Our results demonstrate that as task-switching costs rise, groups increasingly evolve division of labor strategies.

verdict: The evidence is mixed, showing that while multitasking can impair cognitive outcomes and increase susceptibility to interference, it is also associated with improved task-switching abilities in certain contexts.
caveat: The research shows significant heterogeneity in outcomes, including conflicting results on whether media multitasking improves or impairs task-switching ability.
caption:
Your brain is changing to accommodate a life of constant digital input.

Research shows that while heavy media multitasking is linked to a reduced ability to filter out interference, it is also associated with improved task-switching abilities in specific contexts. The evidence remains mixed and contested.
